source_batch.unit_label: Module A: International Banking - Documentary Letters of Credit

facts.statement: The International Chamber of Commerce (ICC), established in 1919 and headquartered in Paris, frames the Uniform Customs and Practice for Documentary Credits (UCPDC), which were first brought out in 1933 and revised in 1951, 1962, 1974, 1983, 1993 and 2007. The current version is UCP 600 (ICC publication No. 600), effective 1 July 2007.

Successive revisions added: the term "applicant" and the methods of settlement (1951); the principle that parties deal in documents and not in goods (1951); that the credit is separate from the sales contract and the confirming bank negotiates without recourse (1962); "nomination" (1974); a requirement of reasonable care to check authenticity, deferred payment undertakings and a definition of transhipment (1983); a credit is irrevocable if silent, a reasonable time not exceeding 7 banking days to examine documents, and disregard of non-documentary conditions (UCP 500, 1993); definitions and interpretations articles, removal of reference to revocable credits and a maximum examination period of 5 banking days following the day of presentation (UCP 600).

A documentary credit is a signed or authenticated instrument issued by the buyer's banker, embodying an undertaking to pay a stated amount against presentation of documents evidencing shipment and complying with the credit terms. The parties are the applicant (buyer, on whose behalf it is opened); the beneficiary (seller); the issuing or opening bank, which establishes the credit; the advising bank in the seller's country, which authenticates and advises it as the issuing bank's agent; the confirming bank, if any, which undertakes to pay on behalf of the issuing bank; the negotiating or nominated bank, which negotiates and pays the beneficiary; and the reimbursing bank, which reimburses the negotiating or confirming bank.

An irrevocable credit cannot be amended or cancelled without the agreement of all parties, especially the opener, the beneficiary and any confirming bank; all credits issued subject to UCP 600, unless otherwise specified, are irrevocable. A confirmed credit carries an additional undertaking by a bank other than the issuing bank, usually in the exporter's country; the confirming bank steps into the shoes of the issuing bank and has no obligation to add confirmation to later amendments. A transferable credit, which must specifically say so, can be transferred in full or in part to one or more second beneficiaries, but a second beneficiary cannot transfer it again.

A red clause credit allows the beneficiary to draw an advance before shipment, against a written undertaking to deliver the transport documents; a green clause credit is similar but also requires a document proving the goods have been warehoused. Under a sight credit the beneficiary is paid on presenting conforming documents; under a usance (acceptance) credit a draft is drawn payable at a future date, which may run from the date of shipment or the date of the bill of exchange; a deferred payment credit has no draft, with the due date stated in the credit; under a negotiation credit the nominated bank gives value for the documents or draft.

A back-to-back credit is one a beneficiary of an export credit arranges to be issued in favour of a local supplier on the strength of that export credit. A standby letter of credit is similar to a guarantee: the seller can invoke it with a declaration that the customer failed to meet its obligations; it is governed by UCP or by the International Standby Practices ISP 98, and is a guarantee against default rather than a payment instrument. A revolving credit covers consecutive instalments of a contract for delivery at intervals; the second instalment is not effective until the first has been paid.

In an export credit flow the buyer's bank sends the credit by SWIFT (message MT 700) to the exporter's bank or another bank with which it has correspondent relations; the receiving bank authenticates and advises it. After shipment the exporter submits the documents to the nominated bank, which scrutinises them and may negotiate or forward them to the issuing bank. The issuing bank scrutinises them independently and, if compliant, delivers them to the importer against payment (sight) or acceptance (usance), and pays by remitting funds to the Nostro account of the nominated bank (message MT 202) or conveys its acceptance by SWIFT.

payload.title: Why a seller trusts a bank instead of a stranger
payload.core_explanation_md:
A seller in one country and a buyer in another do not know each other. The **documentary credit** closes the gap: the **buyer's bank** promises to pay the seller **if** the seller presents the **documents** the credit asks for, within the time stated, and complying with every term.

Two ideas run through the whole subject:
- The banks deal in **documents, not goods**. They pay or refuse on what the papers say, not on what is in the container.
- The credit is **separate from the sales contract**. A dispute about the goods does not change what the bank must do on conforming documents.

The rules that make this work are written by the **International Chamber of Commerce** (founded 1919, Paris). The set is the **UCPDC**, first issued in 1933 and revised in 1951, 1962, 1974, 1983, 1993 and **2007**. Today's edition is **UCP 600**, effective **1 July 2007**.

payload.title: What each revision added: a memory ladder
payload.core_explanation_md:
A short ladder helps recall which version brought which idea.

- **1951**: the word **applicant**; the settlement methods; **banks deal in documents, not goods**.
- **1962**: the credit is **separate from the sales contract**; a confirming bank negotiates **without recourse**.
- **1974**: **nomination**.
- **1983**: duty of **reasonable care on authenticity**; **deferred payment**; definition of **transhipment**.
- **1993 (UCP 500)**: a credit is **irrevocable if silent**; **reasonable time not exceeding 7 banking days** to examine documents; **non-documentary conditions disregarded**.
- **2007 (UCP 600)**: articles on **definitions** and **interpretations**; **no more revocable credits**; examination in a maximum of **5 banking days following the day of presentation**.

The move from **7** days to **5** days between UCP 500 and UCP 600 is a favourite exam point.

payload.title: Seven parties, one question each
payload.core_explanation_md:
Ask of every party: **whom does it act for, and what does it do?**

- **Applicant** (the buyer/importer): asks for the credit to be opened.
- **Issuing (opening) bank**: the applicant's bank, which **establishes** the credit and carries the primary payment promise.
- **Beneficiary** (the seller/exporter): gets paid if the documents comply.
- **Advising bank**: in the seller's country, acts as the issuing bank's **agent**, **authenticates** the credit and tells the beneficiary.
- **Confirming bank**: adds **its own** undertaking to pay, standing beside the issuing bank.
- **Nominated (negotiating) bank**: **negotiates** the documents and pays the beneficiary.
- **Reimbursing bank**: **reimburses** the negotiating or confirming bank.

One bank can wear several hats. The advising, confirming and negotiating banks may all be the same bank.

payload.title: Irrevocable, confirmed, transferable: three words, three different protections
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Irrevocable**: cannot be changed or cancelled unless **all** parties agree, the opener, the beneficiary and any confirming bank. Under UCP 600 credits are **irrevocable** unless they say otherwise, and the earlier idea of a **revocable** credit was removed in 2007.

**Confirmed**: a **second bank** (usually in the exporter's country) adds its **own** undertaking. It steps into the issuing bank's shoes. It is **not obliged to confirm later amendments**, and must tell the beneficiary if it will not.

**Transferable**: the credit must **say so**. It can pass in whole or in part to one or more **second beneficiaries**, but a second beneficiary **cannot transfer it again**.

The three answer different worries: **changes** (irrevocable), **the issuing bank's credit risk or country risk** (confirmed) and **the beneficiary is a middleman** (transferable).

payload.title: Paying for goods before they ship, and paying later: the special credits
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Advance before shipment**
- **Red clause**: the beneficiary can draw an **advance** against a written undertaking to deliver the transport documents later.
- **Green clause**: the same, but the advance also needs a **document showing the goods are warehoused**, so it is a little safer for the bank.

**When the money moves**
- **Sight**: paid when conforming documents are presented.
- **Usance (acceptance)**: a **draft** is drawn payable at a future date, counted from a stated point such as the shipment date or the draft date.
- **Deferred payment**: **no draft**; the due date is simply stated in the credit.
- **Negotiation**: the nominated bank **gives value** for the documents or draft.

**Credits that sit on other credits**
- **Back-to-back**: a middleman uses an export credit to support a **local supplier credit**.
- **Revolving**: covers **consecutive instalments** of a delivery contract; the second instalment is not effective until the first is paid.

payload.title: The standby credit: a promise that is hoped never to be used
payload.core_explanation_md:
A **standby letter of credit** looks like a credit but behaves like a **guarantee**. It is a safeguard against **default**, not a payment instrument.

- If the customer fails to pay or perform, the beneficiary **claims** by presenting a **declaration** (with whatever other documents the standby asks for) that the customer failed.
- It is governed by **UCP** or by the **International Standby Practices, ISP 98**.

Compare with a **documentary credit**: there, the seller expects to use it on every shipment. With a standby, the happy ending is that it **expires unused**.

payload.title: When does a 90-day usance draft fall due?
payload.core_explanation_md: Illustrative case: a usance credit requires a draft payable 90 days from the date of shipment. The goods are shipped on 18 January 2026. The issuing bank accepts the draft. On what date is payment due, and how many days of each month are counted?

worked_steps.description: Days left in January after the shipment date.
Days still needed to reach 90, counted into April.

self_check.prompt_text: If the same draft were payable 90 days from the date of the bill of exchange and the draft is dated 25 January 2026, would the due date be earlier or later?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Later: counting starts a week later, so the date moves to 25 April 2026.

unresolved: The courseware (printed pp. 92-93) still describes the revocable credit as a type; UCP 600 removed it and the courseware itself says all UCP 600 credits are irrevocable. The items teach the irrevocable position and mention the removal.

The ICC academy page on documentary credits (read through a fetch; the page blocked a direct download so it is not saved or fingerprinted) corroborates that UCP 600 is the 2007 revision. It also shows ISBP 821 (July 2023) and URR 725 as current, which bears on the later ISBP 745 batch.

The flow of an export or import credit through RBI systems (EDPMS, IDPMS, shipping bill, bill of entry) on printed pp. 95-98 is not taught here; it belongs to the exporter and importer facilities unit.
